text: More recently, LLM-augmented Bayesian models have extended discrete hypothesis updating by incorporating qualitative signals from natural-language utterances, using Luce's Choice Axiom for linguistic likelihoods and normal-distribution likelihoods for numerical offers, fused through Bayesian updating ([6.1], [6.2]).

The comprehensive survey by Baarslag et al. 2016 catalogues the following accuracy metrics: Euclidean distance on issue weights, mean squared error and mean absolute error on predicted bid utilities, Pearson correlation for preference rankings, and percentage error for reservation-value and deadline estimates ([3.3], [3.4]).

On the performance side, models are evaluated by negotiation-outcome metrics: average utility, distance to the Pareto frontier, distance to a fair solution (Nash or Kalai–Smorodinsky), agreement percentage, and joint utility ([3.5], [3.6]).
The survey explicitly notes that accuracy metrics for reservation-value and deadline estimators remain underdeveloped ([3.7]).
Cui and Lin 2025 introduced BOND (Bayesian Opponent-belief Negotiation Distillation), which reports turn-level Brier scores for opponent-type prediction in the CaSiNo negotiation domain.

The Bayesian teacher achieved a mean Brier score of 0.085 on 1,054 predictions, compared to 0.114 for the distilled student and 0.194 for a chain-ofthought baseline—the first use of a proper scoring rule for opponent beliefs in negotiation ([7.1], [7.2],
Sicilia et al. 2024 proposed FortUne Dial, evaluating negotiation-outcome forecasting across eight corpora using Brier score and Brier skill score, with explicit calibration analysis ([8.1], [8.2]).

section: 3. Decomposition of Uncertainty: Aleatoric vs. Epistemic
text: The Baarslag et al. 2016 survey frames uncertainty purely as incomplete knowledge of the opponent's private preferences and strategy—what would formally be epistemic uncertainty —without separating it from irreducible randomness in opponent behavior ([3.7], [3.8]).

section: 3. Decomposition of Uncertainty: Aleatoric vs. Epistemic
text: Adversarial Risk Analysis (Banks et al., 2022) explicitly separates aleatory uncertainty (randomness in outcomes conditional on both parties' choices) from epistemic uncertainty (incomplete knowledge of the opponent's utility function, beliefs, and resources).

section: 3. Decomposition of Uncertainty: Aleatoric vs. Epistemic
text: UAOM (Yang et al., 2025) provides an explicit aleatoric–epistemic decomposition in deep RL opponent modeling, using a hybrid of deterministic and probabilistic encoders: the probabilistic component captures behavioral randomness (aleatoric), while the ensemble of models captures knowledge limitations (epistemic) ([10.1], [10.2], [10.3]).

text: No work was found that estimates the value of perfect information specifically about the counterpart's reservation value, though Hendrikx 2012 benchmarks performance under perfect knowledge of the full preference profile as an upper bound ([11.1], [12.1]).

Hindriks and Tykhonov 2008 describe a spread parameter σ controlling how aggressively the posterior updates: lower σ reflects greater prior confidence and produces faster learning, while higher σ reflects uncertainty and makes updating less aggressive ([13.1]).
Eshragh's 2019 particlefilter approach demonstrates improved opponent estimates over rounds, but without formal convergence guarantees ([14.1], [4.3]).
The GP model of Leahu et al. 2019 updates beliefs as interaction data accumulate, but does not establish convergence conditions ([5.1]).
When the opponent uses a Boulware strategy (β < 1), concessions are withheld until near the deadline, providing minimal information for most of the session ([2.1]).

Against behavior-dependent or strategic opponents who condition their offers on the agent's behavior, the stationarity assumption underlying most models is violated, and the posterior may converge to the wrong value ([13.1]).

Baarslag et al. 2016 note that existing reservation-value and deadline estimators are narrowly scoped, typically assuming that the form of the opponent's decision function is known while only its parameters are unknown; extending these methods to arbitrary strategies and initially unknown preferences is described as an open problem ([3.7]).

Under some models, reservation value and deadline are structurally related—the opponent concedes toward reservation value as the deadline approaches—so one may be derivable from the other rather than independently identified ([3.9]).

Zhang et al. 2025 note that observed offers may reflect both the underlying reserve and behavioral parameters such as concession willingness, and that a fully developed Bayesian dynamic model would be needed to disentangle them ([15.1]).

text: Liu et al. 2026 model concurrent multi-buyer bargaining as a finite-horizon exploration–exploitation problem: a seller with a limited message budget must decide whether to use communication turns for diagnostic probing (exploration) to discover hidden buyer valuations, or to concentrate on a promising buyer (exploitation).

Their RLVR-trained seller learns strategic probing and price anchoring as mechanisms for gathering information while influencing counterparties' offers, substantially outperforming frontier LLMs that fixate on the current highest bid ([17.1], [17.2], [17.3]).
Behavioral evidence for offers-as-experiments comes from Ding and Lehrer 2026, who study bilateral bargaining with gradual information revelation.
The theoretical model predicts extensive experimentation, but laboratory subjects experiment far less than predicted, with fairness preferences substantially reducing probing behavior ([18.1],

The GP-based negotiation model of Leahu et al. 2019 frames preference elicitation as an action with an expected information gain that must exceed its "bother" cost, providing a value-of-information interpretation for information-gathering actions during negotiation ([5.3]).
The UCB and Thompson Sampling algorithms possess natural robustness properties for exploration under uncertainty in sequential decision problems with auxiliary information (Gur and Momeni, 2022).

In nonstationary RL settings, Cheung et al. 2023 introduce "confidence widening"—adding additional optimism beyond the conventional UCB exploration bonus—to handle environments where historical data may be misleading, achieving improved dynamic regret bounds.

The linear anchoring effect on price persists independently of impasse risk, suggesting it operates through cognitive adjustment rather than information revelation ([22.1]).

Ames and Mason 2015 distinguish informational and politeness effects of range offers, finding that range offers can signal the offer-maker's reservation price and influence counterpart judgments of rudeness and reservation price ([23.1]).

Ding and Lehrer's 2026 experimental evidence on screening offers comes closest, showing that intermediate offers function as costly experiments that accelerate belief updating, but this operates through seller acceptance/rejection rather than anchoring ([18.1]).

Exact computation requires evaluating 2^N coalitions, making it exponential in the number of models; sampling approximations (Random Order Value, permutation sampling) reduce this to polynomial cost with probabilistic guarantees ([22.4]).
Li et al. 2021 apply Shapley values to multi-agent credit assignment in cooperative RL, using Monte Carlo sampling to make computation tractable.

Difference rewards and counterfactual baselines (Wolpert and Tumer, 2002) assign each agent the difference between the global reward and a counterfactual reward computed by replacing that agent's action with a default.
COMA (Foerster et al., 2018) implements this via a centralized critic that marginalizes out a single agent's action while keeping others fixed.
Stacking (Wolpert, 1992; Breiman, 1996) learns combination weights by minimizing cross-validated loss, making fewer assumptions than BMA about model correctness.

Li et al. 2021 combine Shapley structure with counterfactual baselines in "Shapley Counterfactual Credits," using Shapley's coalition-averaging to improve upon single-counterfactual difference rewards.

The ambiguity decomposition (Krogh and Vedelsby, 1995) shows that the mean squared error of a weighted ensemble decomposes as: ensemble error = mean individual error − ambiguity, where ambiguity measures the weighted variance of individual predictions around the ensemble prediction.
Brown and Wyatt 2003 extended this decomposition and showed that Negative Correlation Learning can explicitly optimize the tradeoff between individual accuracy and diversity.
Audhkhasi et al. 2013 proposed a Generalized Ambiguity Decomposition extending the result beyond squared loss.
Lee et al. 2024 propose HyRe, which dynamically reweights ensemble members at test time using a small set of labeled examples, maintaining diversity through regularization.
L2 regularization of ensemble weights has been shown to preserve broader weight distribution across models and improve performance in COVID-19 forecasting ensembles (Stephens et al., 2023).

The COVID-19 Forecast Hub evaluation (Cramer et al., 2022) found that a simple equally-weighted median ensemble performed better than 83% of participating models for incident cases (N=886 predictions from 23 models) and 91% for deaths (N=763 from 20 models) across 32 European countries over 52 weeks.
For influenza forecasting, McAndrew and Reich 2021 developed an adaptive stacking ensemble that updates weights week-by-week using regularized likelihood.

Tsang et al. 2024 report that an Adaptive Weight Blending Ensemble (AWBE) for influenza in Hong Kong reduced RMSE by 52% and WIS by 53%, substantially outperforming both individual models and a simple average ensemble.

Stephens et al. 2023 found that for COVID-19 mortality, a performance-based ensemble with L2 regularization outperformed a baseline mean ensemble across US states on both absolute error and weighted interval scores, but emphasized that "sufficient regularization and constraints" are essential to prevent overfitting of weights—consistent with the diversity-preservation principle.

section: 6. Credit Assignment with Delayed and Partial Feedback
text: The adaptive ensemble approaches in forecast hubs (McAndrew and Reich, 2021; Tsang et al., 2024) update weights based on recently resolved outcomes, implementing a form of temporal credit with recency weighting.

section: 6. Credit Assignment with Delayed and Partial Feedback
text: The adaptive multi-model ensemble of Fiandrino et al. 2026 applies a particle-filtering approach to epidemic projections, dynamically selecting individual model trajectories based on observed data throughout the projection period—a form of sequential credit assignment with partial feedback.
